title: The bodhisattva precepts
hookLine: in East Asia and Tibet many lay people take bodhisattva vows as well as the five precepts
tomorrow: Taking vows as a lay person
last: UPOSATHA: A DAY LIVED AS THE AWAKENED LIVE.

lines: THE FIVE PRECEPTS DRAW A LINE.
WHAT YOU WILL DO FOR OTHERS.
cards: The five precepts are mostly about what you don't do. Don't kill, don't steal, don't lie. You met them early on, and the line they draw around your own conduct matters.
But in East Asia and in Tibet, monks and lay people alike can take a second set of vows on top of the five.
These ask something different: what you'll do for others, and what you'll refuse to do to them even in your heart.
A Zen student, a grandmother at a temple in Taiwan, a Tibetan family at a ceremony with their lama: each might hold these vows. Today, the bodhisattva precepts.

teach.h: A BEING SET ON AWAKENING FOR ALL.
teach.b: A bodhisattva is a being set on awakening, not only for themselves but for everyone. The bodhisattva precepts are the rules of that kind of life.
In China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, a widely used set comes from a text called the Brahma's Net Sutra: ten major precepts and forty-eight minor ones.
The first few sound familiar: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no lying, no selling intoxicants. But listen to how they stretch.

Not only don't kill, the text says, but don't encourage killing, don't praise it, don't make the means for it, and keep a heart of compassion that wants to protect life. Then come precepts the five never mention.
Don't spread the faults of fellow Buddhists. Don't praise yourself while putting others down. Don't be stingy when someone asks for help, even with a teaching.
Don't hold on to anger when someone apologizes. That last one is worth a pause. It isn't only don't hit back.
In Tibet, the bodhisattva vow comes through a different line of texts and teachers, with its own list, but the turn is the same: the vow faces outward. The five precepts protect others from you.
The bodhisattva precepts ask you to stand up for them. Some ceremonies also include three short pure precepts: avoid harm, do good, and help all beings.
Not just a fence around your own life, but a promise about everyone else's.

how: In East Asian Buddhism, monks, nuns and lay people may receive the bodhisattva precepts of the Brahma's Net Sutra in a ceremony, and in Tibetan Buddhism the bodhisattva vow is given by a lama; both are taken in addition to the five precepts.

o: vows facing outward: protect, help and forgive, not just avoid harm
the rules a monk follows inside the monastery walls each day
a stricter copy of the five precepts, kept only by monks

the East Asian source of the precepts

s: the bodhisattva precepts are only for monks and nuns
in East Asia and Tibet, lay people take them too, on top of the five.
the Brahma's Net Sutra lists ten major precepts
ten major and forty-eight minor, in the text itself.
one precept is not to refuse an apology
holding on to anger when someone asks forgiveness breaks a major precept.

games.q: someone who hurt you comes back and apologizes. under the Brahma's Net Sutra, what's the precept?
o: you may accept, if you feel like it.
don't hold on to anger; receive the apology.
stay polite but keep your distance forever.
games.why: the text counts refusing an apology and holding on to anger among the major precepts. the vow faces outward.

practice: Hold one precept from the Brahma's Net Sutra, in plain words: don't hold on to anger when someone asks to be forgiven.

Let one person come to mind who has said sorry to you, or tried to, maybe clumsily, and notice what happens in your chest and shoulders. No need to fix it; just notice whether the apology has been received yet.

wordCard.voice: The bodhisattva precepts. Vows taken on top of the five, facing outward: not only don't harm, but protect, help and forgive. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit bodhisattva (Pali bodhisatta): a being set on awakening; in the Mahayana, one who seeks it for all beings.

carryVoice: Your line: vows for others. Sometimes keeping one is as quiet as not adding to someone's fault being discussed. Until tomorrow, friend.
